newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries up after payrolls but off highs.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries up after payrolls but off highs.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices were higher in early afternoon trade on Friday as the market registered relief that U.S. January employment data were benign enough to put off any Federal Reserve rate tightening.
The market had conceded nearly half of its best gains, however, as buyers proved unwilling to push into higher territory without any sign that the U.S. economy was actually weakening.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 24/32 in early afternoon trade, yielding 6.70 percent.
Earlier, the 30-year Treasury bond was up more than a point, its yield falling as low as 6.67 percent.
Analysts said several factors worked to constrain the market's advance.

First, while job growth in January was less robust than the financial markets' worst fears, it was far from weak. The Labor Department reported non-farm payrolls swelled by 271,000 new jobs in January after December growth of 261,000 new jobs.
And the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) linked the sharp drop in the length of the average workweek to 34.1 hours in January from 34.8 hours in December to harsh winter weather.

Rubin told a news conference at midday that he supported a strong dollar but added that the U.S. currency has been strong "for some time now." He said he expected foreign exchange issues to be a "principal topic" of discussion at Saturday's meeting of G7 economic policymakers from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
"Some G7 countries have expressed concern about the recent declines in their currencies," Rubin said. "We look forward to discussing these issues in Germany."
Analysts said Rubin's comments sparked profit-taking in the dollar, which in turn pressured Treasury prices.
After rising to 113-00, a 50 percent retracement of a two-month downmove, March T-bond futures backtracked, triggering stops at 112-19 and retreating to 112-12.

A $39.75 billion Treasury refunding operation as well as noteworthy economic data on January retail sales, producer prices and industrial production, all on next week's calendar, were also considerations that helped to take the sizzle out of the market's early rally, analysts said.
In afternoon trade, the Treasury's three-month bill rate was unchanged at 5.00 percent, exactly where it was before the payroll data that spurred the market higher.
Six-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.06 percent. Year bill Treasury rates were off four basis points to 5.20 percent.
Two-year notes were up 2/32 to 100 even, yielding 5.87 percent. Five-year notes were up 5/32 to 100-9/32, yielding 6.18 percent.
Ten-year notes were up 7/32 to 100-15/32, yielding 6.43 percent.
